notes.meaning: Four royal officials heard what Jeremiah was saying. He was locked in the courtyard of the guard, but people could still come and listen to him. His body was held, but God's word was not chained. Gedaliah was probably the son of the Pashhur who had once put Jeremiah in the stocks.

Jeremiah kept giving the same hard message from God. Jerusalem would surely fall to the Babylonians, here called the Chaldeans. Anyone who stayed would die by war, hunger or disease. Anyone who gave themselves up would live, like someone escaping a shipwreck who saves only their life and loses everything else. The words "he will live" are repeated to urge the people even more strongly.

The officials asked the king to put Jeremiah to death. They said he was "weakening the hands" of the soldiers, which means taking away their courage. His words did make people less willing to fight. But the charge was unfair. He was speaking God's word out of love, so that the people would not be wiped out. It is common for wicked people to treat God's faithful messengers as enemies.

Zedekiah was a weak king who was afraid of his own officials. He knew Jeremiah was God's true prophet, but he did not have the courage to protect him. So he handed him over and said he could do nothing to stop them. He gave up an innocent man to his own weakness and to their hatred.

They lowered Jeremiah on ropes into a deep, empty water pit. Only mud was left at the bottom, and he sank into it. They meant for him to die slowly there, so they could tell themselves they had not shed his blood. Jeremiah later remembered calling on God from that pit, and God drew near to him. Some see him here as a picture of Christ, who also suffered for being faithful.

Help came from someone no one would expect. Ebed-melech was a foreigner from Cush, which is Ethiopia, and he served in the palace. His name means "king's servant." He went straight to the king, who was sitting at the city gate to hear cases, and spoke up in public. That took real courage. God can raise up friends for his people in surprising places.

Ebed-melech told the king plainly that the officials had done evil to Jeremiah, even though they were powerful men. He called Jeremiah "the prophet" to show how wrong it was. With almost no bread left in the city, no one would feed a man left in a pit, so he would starve. This outsider showed more kindness than all of Jeremiah's own people.

The king who had just said he could do nothing now changed his mind. He told Ebed-melech to take thirty men and pull Jeremiah out. So many men were sent to guard the rescue in case the officials tried to stop it. The king's heart is in God's hand, so we can be encouraged to stand up boldly for what is right.

Ebed-melech found old rags and worn-out clothes in a storeroom of the palace. He lowered them carefully on ropes instead of throwing them down, so they would not be lost in the mud. God can use the plainest, humblest things to do good to his people.

The rags were padding, so the ropes would not cut into Jeremiah's armpits as he was hauled up. Jeremiah did as he was told and was pulled out. Small acts of kindness like this are not forgotten by God. Jeremiah was not set free but went back to the courtyard of the guard. That was actually the safest place for him, away from his enemies.

Zedekiah secretly met Jeremiah at an entrance to the temple. He asked for a word from God and told him to hide nothing. He had already heard the answer before. He seems to have been hoping for a nicer one, as if God might change his mind. He feared God a little but would not truly obey him.

Jeremiah was careful. He knew the king could have him killed for telling the truth, and that the king had ignored his advice again and again. The second part is best read as a sad statement: "you will not listen to me." Jeremiah was not afraid to die for God. He simply saw no point in risking his life for advice that would be thrown away.

The king swore a solemn, secret oath by the living God, who gives everyone life. He was saying, in effect, "May I lose my life if I deceive you." He promised not to kill Jeremiah or hand him to the officials. But he made no promise to listen.

Jeremiah gave the same message as before, in God's name, not as his own opinion. If Zedekiah surrendered to Babylon's generals, he and his family would live and the city would not be burned. The generals are named because the king of Babylon himself was elsewhere. It was a great mercy that God still offered this to such a stubborn king.
Then came the warning. If he refused, the city would be captured and burned, and he would not escape. God set before him life and death. People must either bend before God or break.

Zedekiah admitted his real fear. He was afraid of the Jews who had already gone over to Babylon, and that they would mock and mistreat him. He feared people more than he feared God. Faithful people feel fear too, but they bring it to God and obey anyway. Zedekiah let his fear win.

Jeremiah promised that this would not happen. He pleaded with the king to obey the Lord's voice so that things would go well and he would live. God was inviting him to leave his worry in God's hands. What God tells us is always for our good, even when it is hard to hear.

If he refused, God showed Jeremiah a scene. The women of the palace would be led out to Babylon's officers and would sing a mocking song about him. The song says his "friends," his advisers and false prophets, led him astray, got his feet stuck in the mud, and then ran off. Zedekiah feared mockery from men but would face mockery from women. Getting stuck in mud also echoes what was done to Jeremiah.

His wives and children would be taken, and he himself would be captured. Jeremiah says Zedekiah himself will burn the city. That does not mean he would light the fire. It means the blame would be his, because he refused to obey God. Rulers' pride often brings suffering on their people.

Zedekiah had nothing to say against the advice, but he would not follow it. He told Jeremiah to keep their talk secret, or he could lose his life. He wanted it hidden mostly to protect his own name with the officials. His fear showed he believed Jeremiah, yet he chose to keep living in dread.

The king expected the officials to come asking questions. He told Jeremiah to say he had been humbly begging not to be sent back to Jonathan's house to die. Jonathan's house was the terrible prison he had been kept in before. The king, who should have ruled, was afraid of his own officials.

The officials did come. Jeremiah told them only what the king had told him to say. Since no one had overheard the meeting, they left him alone. Christians have long asked whether Jeremiah did right here.

differ.view: Jeremiah reports what he did but does not praise it. His answer hid the main thing and was a kind of falsehood that cannot be fully excused, a weakness born of fear.
What he said was true, though not the whole truth. He was not bound to say more, since God had not commanded him to and the king had forbidden it.
It was the truth and nothing but the truth, though not the whole truth. No one has to reveal everything to people who have no right to know it.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah stayed a prisoner in the courtyard of the guard until the day Jerusalem fell. He was not freed by his own people but stayed bound until the city was taken, just as he had said it would be. The way things turned out proved he was a true prophet. In the meantime, God made the prison a place of safety for him.
